abstract: Free fatty acids (FFAs) are the adult heart's primary energy substrate, but human cardiac lipid exchange remains incompletely characterized. We assessed cardiac lipid import and export using arteriovenous lipidomics in a prospective observational study of 59 fasting patients undergoing catheter ablation for atrial arrhythmias. Paired arterial and coronary sinus plasma samples underwent targeted lipidomics, detecting 1,464 lipid species across 20 classes; 851 species were analyzed. Paired comparisons used separate Benjamini-Hochberg corrections for classes and species. The heart showed net uptake of FFAs (-122.4 μmol/L; 95% confidence interval [CI], -146.0 to -98.8; q = 1.49 × 10⁻13) and nonsignificant triglyceride uptake. Lysophosphatidylcholine was released (+4.32 μmol/L; 95% CI, 2.45 to 6.19; q = 2.12 × 10⁻⁴); no other class met q < 0.05. Thirty-two species met q < 0.05. Release from other classes offset FFA and triglyceride uptake on average, yielding a positive aggregate acyl-chain-equivalent difference (+28.2 μmol acyl-chain equivalents/L), although the CI included both uptake and release (95% CI, -112.8 to 169.2; P = 0.690). This study characterizes distinct patterns of cardiac lipid exchange under fasting conditions and provides a basis for studies in heart failure and broader cardiometabolic disease. Further studies are warranted to identify the sources of released lipids and explore cardiac lipid handling in the fed state.
